newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine security chief worried about Russia ties.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine security chief worried about Russia ties.

text.p: Ukraine's security chief on Saturday expressed fears on the eve of a high-profile visit to Washington that uncertainty over ailing Kremlin leader Boris Yeltsin's future was hurting his country's relations with Russia.

Volodymyr Horbulin, secretary of Ukraine's Security Council, told a news conference he opposed any suggestion that the United States might act as a go-between in Ukraine's main dispute with Russia -- the division of the Black Sea Fleet.

Horbulin was speaking after Russian politicians with an eye on Yeltsin's forthcoming heart surgery reopened debate on the ownership of the fleet and the city of Sevastopol, site of its main base in Ukraine's largely pro-Russian Crimean peninsula.
"We said that pressure would increase on Ukraine from all sides after (June's Russian presidential) election. And this is exactly what has happened," Horbulin said.

"It is uncertain just who we are to deal with. There are too many people with titles involved. Proposals for U.S. help as an intermediary often come up. I am personally against this as it would show us to be helpless."

The United States served as an intermediary in a 1994 agreement under which Ukraine agreed to give up its share of former Soviet nuclear weapons to Russia in exchange for about $1 billion in compensation.

Horbulin's week-long U.S. visit includes meetings with Defence Secretary William Perry, National Security Adviser Anthony Lake and the heads of the Central Intelligence Agency and Federal Bureau of Investigation.

His influence on government policy has long been acknowledged, but Horbulin has lately adopted a more public approach, perhaps in response to that undertaken by his Russian opposite number, Alexander Lebed.

Ukrainian officials, who backed Yeltsin's re-election bid, are clearly worried about how a president weakened by heart surgery, or a race to succeed Yeltsin, would affect relations between the two most powerful former Soviet republics.
"It's like traditional Russian operas of intrigue and power brokering," said one senior official. "You don't know who you're dealing with. No one really holds the reins of power."

The dispute over the Black Sea Fleet remains the sole hurdle preventing signature of a friendship treaty five years into the post-Soviet era. The two sides have agreed on splitting the 900 ships but are divided over how to divide bases in Crimea, populated mainly by ethnic Russians.

Lebed said this week Sevastopol could not be considered part of Ukraine as it was not included in a 1954 order by Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev transferring Crimea from Russian to Ukrainian control.
Moscow Mayor Yuri Luzhkov, a possible contender in any Russian presidential race, said it was the "simple truth that Sevastopol is a Russian city which we...will never give up".

Ukrainian President Leonid Kuchma, who since his 1994 election has overseen an improvement in initially rocky post-Soviet relations with Russia, said: "If president Yeltsin were healthy, none of these discussions would be taking place."
Relations have also skidded on other fronts.
Russia this week went ahead with the imposition of a tax on Ukrainian sugar imports despite warnings by Kuchma that this would mark the beginning of a trade war.
